title: Checkpoint: The Social Animal
objective: After this level you can explain how other people shape what we believe and do, and which famous studies need caution.
summary: Other people push us to conform, obey and stand by, but we are not puppets: people follow causes they believe in and resist bare orders. Some famous studies held up; others need their criticisms told.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: other people move us, but not like puppets.
cards.body: This chapter's groups bent answers, orders pushed people on, and crowds held back. Yet the closer researchers looked, the more people seemed to follow causes they believed in, not just commands. First, a fresh look at obedience; then every study, sorted.

cards.headline: Obeying a cause, not an order
cards.body: Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher reanalyzed the classic studies. In Milgram's lab, people tended to continue when prodded in the name of the science ("The experiment requires that you continue") but typically refused a bare order ("You have no other choice, you must go on"). They argue that people follow authorities when they identify with them and believe they're right. Obedience, on this view, is less about blind habit and more about shared belief.

items.label: Held up
points: One dissenter weakened conformity in Asch's studies
Crowds do dilute each person's sense of duty

items.label: Needed correcting
points: Stanford's guards were pushed to be tough
The 38 silent witnesses story was inaccurate
On camera, someone helped in 9 of 10 real conflicts

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How groups and authorities push us to conform, obey or stand by, and what weakens that pull.
Why the Milgram and Stanford studies must be taught together with their criticisms.
What dissonance, persuasion and minimal groups reveal about how minds and loyalties shift.
Why findings from WEIRD samples may not describe people everywhere.

questions.prompt: The Social Animal recap: which kind of instruction did Milgram's participants typically refuse?

options.label: A request to keep going for the sake of the experiment
options.rationale: Appeals to the science tended to keep people going.

options.label: A polite "please continue"
A bare order saying they had no other choice
An explanation of how the shock machine worked
options.rationale: That wasn't an instruction to continue.

questions.explanation: According to Haslam and Reicher, participants typically refused the direct order "You have no other choice, you must go on".

questions.prompt: The Social Animal recap: why do Haslam and Reicher see people who follow harmful orders as more than blind conformists?

options.label: They follow when they identify with the authority and believe it is right
They follow only when they are paid enough
They follow because they cannot see what they are doing
options.rationale: They argue followers act knowingly, from belief.

options.label: They follow only when a crowd is watching
options.rationale: Their account is about identification, not audiences.

questions.explanation: Their reanalysis argues that following depends on identifying with the authority and believing its cause is right.

questions.prompt: The Social Animal recap, from Level 71: what made conformity drop sharply in Asch's line studies?

options.label: Adding more people to the majority
options.rationale: That raised conformity, up to a point.

options.label: Making participants answer out loud
Paying participants for correct answers
options.rationale: That wasn't one of the factors studied.

options.label: One other person breaking with the majority

questions.explanation: A single dissenter from the majority made conformity drop sharply.

questions.prompt: The Social Animal recap, from Level 74: what does the evidence now say about bystanders?

options.label: The 38 silent witnesses story proved people never help
options.rationale: That story turned out to be inaccurate.

options.label: Each person holds back more in a crowd, yet someone usually helps
Crowds make every individual more likely to help
options.rationale: In the lab, each person helped less with others present.

options.label: Bystanders help only when they are alone
options.rationale: On camera, groups usually produced a helper.

questions.explanation: The bystander effect is real for each individual, but in 9 of 10 filmed public conflicts at least one bystander helped.

questions.prompt: The Social Animal recap, from Level 1: Burger repeated part of Milgram's published study in 2009. Which habit of science does that show?

options.label: Relying on one famous result as final
options.rationale: Replication exists because one result isn't final.

options.label: Asking people to introspect about obedience
Others repeating a published test to check it
Studying one person in great depth
options.rationale: That's a case study; Burger tested 70 adults.

questions.explanation: Psychologists publish results so others can replicate or build on them; Burger's partial replication did exactly that.
